network.overall_strategy: This network maps plausible abiotic formation pathways of threonine from simple C1 and C2 feedstocks, integrating hydrothermal and surface prebiotic environments, leveraging Strecker-like cyanohydrin and aminonitrile chemistry, aldol condensations, and subsequent hydrolysis and amination steps. Several pathways use cross-aldol chemistry, different keto acid precursors, hydrothermal reductive amination and surface-catalyzed transformations, providing pathway diversity.

reactions.name: Acetaldehyde synthesis via reduction of CO2
reactions.mechanism: Fischer-Tropsch-type reduction of CO2 with H2 to small organics, guided on sulfide surfaces.
reactions.reasoning: Nickel-iron sulfide minerals facilitate CO2 reduction to C2 organics under hydrothermal vent conditions (Huber & Wächtershäuser, 1997).

reactions.name: Formaldehyde synthesis from CO2 and H2
reactions.mechanism: Partial reduction of CO2 yielding formaldehyde intermediates.
reactions.reasoning: Hydrothermal systems can catalyze the reduction of CO2 to formaldehyde and related C1 species (Cody et al., 2000).

reactions.name: Glycolaldehyde formation via formose reaction
reactions.mechanism: Aldol dimerization of formaldehyde to glycolaldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: The formose reaction, in the presence of divalent cations or clay minerals, produces glycolaldehyde from formaldehyde (Weber, 1998).

reactions.name: Glyceraldehyde formation via glycolaldehyde aldol condensation
reactions.mechanism: Aldol condensation adds another aldehyde unit, forming C3 sugar.
reactions.reasoning: Aldol chemistry on minerals extends to formation of C3 sugars under prebiotic conditions (Kim et al., 2011).

reactions.name: Pyruvic acid synthesis via oxidation of glyceraldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Photooxidation/metal-catalyzed transformation converts sugar aldehydes to alpha-keto acids.
reactions.reasoning: Abiotic oxidation of sugars to alpha-keto acids by UV plus Fe(III) minerals is supported in surface settings (Zhou et al., 2020).

reactions.name: Alanine formation via reductive amination of pyruvic acid
reactions.mechanism: Imine formation from pyruvate and ammonia, followed by reduction to amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Experimental data demonstrates hydrothermal reductive amination of keto acids to amino acids in Fe-Ni-sulfide environments (Huber & Wächtershäuser, 2003).

reactions.name: Acetic acid synthesis from methanal/ethanal oxidation
reactions.mechanism: UV catalyzed oxidation of simple aldehydes to acids on mineral surfaces.
reactions.reasoning: UV-catalyst oxidation on phosphate-rich mineral surfaces can generate C2 carboxylic acids (Patel et al., 2015 - for analogs).

reactions.name: Pyruvic acid Strecker synthesis to aminonitrile
reactions.mechanism: Pyruvic acid, ammonia, and HCN react to form 2-amino-3-oxobutyric acid (Strecker precursor).
reactions.reasoning: Clay-catalyzed Strecker synthesis of amino acid precursors is robust in prebiotic surface environments (Danger et al., 2012).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of aminonitrile to threonine
reactions.reasoning: Hydrolysis of Strecker aminonitriles is a well-accepted final step toward alpha-amino acids; glyceraldehyde can act as a nucleophile adding hydroxyl (Miller, 1953; Pascal et al. 2013).

reactions.name: Serinol formation by amination of glyceraldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Amination of aldehyde group to primary amino alcohol.
reactions.reasoning: Amine addition to aldehydes on mineral surfaces is prebiotically reasonable (Schoonen et al., 2013).

reactions.name: Aldol condensation between acetaldehyde and glycine intermediates
reactions.mechanism: Aldol addition yields C4 backbone for threonine precursor.
reactions.reasoning: Borate minerals enhance aldol stability and promote prebiotic C4 condensation chemistry (Ricardo et al., 2004).

reactions.name: Glycinonitrile synthesis (Strecker) from glycolaldehyde, ammonia, and HCN
reactions.mechanism: Aldehyde undergoes Strecker reaction to give aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Surface-catalyzed Strecker reactions of C2 aldehydes are well demonstrated in prebiotic analogs (Powner et al., 2009).

pathways.name: Formose-sugar aldehyde -> Strecker-aminonitrile -> Hydrolysis Pathway
pathways.description: Starting from CO2, reduction and formose chemistry yield glyceraldehyde. This is further oxidized to pyruvic acid, which undergoes Strecker reaction and aminonitrile hydrolysis to yield threonine.

pathways.name: Aldol-acetaldehyde plus glycinonitrile condensation route
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde generated via Fischer-Tropsch-type chemistry reacts, after surface-catalyzed Strecker formation of glycinonitrile, in a borate-catalyzed aldol condensation to give threonine aminonitrile, hydrolyzed to threonine.

pathways.name: Alanine extension pathway via two-carbon elongation
pathways.description: From CO2 and H2, through aldol and amination steps to alanine, and chain extension with glycolaldehyde/glyceraldehyde units to reach threonine.

pathways.name: Serinol-based pathway
pathways.description: Formose and amination chemistry lead to serinol, which can rearrange and oxidize to the threonine structure via transamination.

pathways.name: Acetic acid-Keto acid pathway
pathways.description: Surface photochemistry converts aldehydes to acetic, then to pyruvic acid, which enters Strecker and hydrolysis steps to threonine.

pathways.name: HCN-driven direct Strecker pathway
pathways.description: HCN and ammonia availability allow direct Strecker formation of key aminonitrile intermediates after C3 sugar formation and subsequent hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Secondary aldol pathway from glycolaldehyde and glyceraldehyde units
pathways.description: Sequential aldol condensations build up C3 and C4 frameworks, then amination and hydrolysis yield threonine.

pathways.name: Direct amination of C3 backbone pathway
pathways.description: Amination of glyceraldehyde leads to serinol, which after oxidation forms threonine backbone.

pathways.name: Chain-elongation via aminonitrile condensation
pathways.description: Glycinonitrile reacts with acetaldehyde in an aldol-like process, followed by hydrolysis to the amino acid.

pathways.name: Formaldehyde-driven side pathway
pathways.description: From CO2 and H2 yielding formaldehyde, which in formose chemistry ultimately supports C4 chain backbone for threonine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: P1 captures a plausible abiotically-inspired formose/Strecker/aminonitrile/hydrolysis sequence, but every reaction along this pathway is unbalanced per the provided check. Notably, rxn_003 (formose step), rxn_008 (Strecker), and rxn_009 (final hydrolysis) show major conservation violations. Adjusting stoichiometry and detailing expected byproduct formation (e.g. water elimination, addition of H2O, O2, or other balancing species) is necessary. Chemistry is conceptually plausible, but these issues undermine overall soundness and target yield.
suggestions: Add missing species/products (e.g. H2O, O2, etc.) to balance reactions.
Re-express hydrolysis, Strecker, and aldol steps explicitly so all atoms are tracked.

This significantly undermines chemical validity. Stoichiometry and mass conservation require revision.
suggestions: Redo atom balances for condensation and hydrolysis steps.
Clarify mechanism and adjust for proper side products.

evaluation.network_feedback: This network includes a broad span of chemically plausible prebiotic pathways for threonine, using realistic reaction classes (formose, aldol, Strecker, hydrolysis, reductive amination). However, not a single reaction step is balanced per the deterministic check, and several intermediates have formula inconsistencies. These atom and charge conservation failures are a critical flaw, precluding confidence in the network's chemical feasibility. Environmental context is generally reasonable, with plausible assignment of surface and hydrothermal settings. To improve, all reactions must be rewritten with balanced equations, correcting formula errors, and explicitly specifying all byproducts and reactant accounting.
